analysis.one_liner: Blocks new climate and air-pollution rules for oil and gas until Russia leaves Ukraine, and revives the Keystone pipeline.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 3 Republican cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would freeze most federal climate and air-pollution actions affecting oil and gas development — including Biden climate executive orders, EPA ozone and particulate standards, methane rules, and federal agencies' social cost of carbon estimates — from passage until 180 days after Russia withdrew all troops from Ukraine, reverting rules to their January 19, 2021 versions in the meantime [S3]. It would also statutorily authorize the Keystone XL pipeline to be built under its 2019 permit, and it would bar federal financial regulators from restricting bank lending to oil and gas companies [S3]. A nonbinding section urges faster natural gas export approvals and more offshore oil and gas lease sales [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers gain the most: the bill suspends the climate executive orders, EPA methane and air-quality rules, FERC pipeline climate reviews, and social cost of carbon accounting that raise their costs, and it hands Keystone XL's developer a statutory permit to build. Banks lending to the sector also gain, since financial regulators would be barred from restricting that lending. Consumers facing high energy prices are the stated beneficiaries, but the link is indirect — oil is priced on world markets, so more U.S. drilling does not automatically lower U.S. pump or heating bills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas producers and pipeline companies

how_it_helps.text: It would nullify the policy underpinnings of federal climate action for oil and gas — Executive Orders 13990 and 14008, EPA's ozone and particulate-matter standards decisions, EPA methane rules, FERC's greenhouse gas pipeline policies, and the government's social cost of carbon estimates — for as long as the covered period lasts [S3].

It would statutorily authorize TransCanada Keystone Pipeline, L.P. to build and operate the border-crossing pipeline under the terms of the March 29, 2019 presidential permit, overriding the permit's revocation without needing any new administrative approval [S3].

It would prohibit the Federal Reserve and other federal financial regulators from taking any action that restricts access to capital or lending for companies in the oil and natural gas subsector [S3].

Its nonbinding section presses the Energy Secretary to speed up liquefied natural gas export approvals, the Interior Secretary to issue a new five-year offshore leasing plan with at least as many lease sales as the 2017-2022 program, and the Attorney General to appeal a court ruling that halted an offshore lease sale [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost: suspending the ozone and fine-particulate air standards allows more smog and soot, pollutants linked to asthma, heart disease, and premature death; reversion to January 19, 2021 rules cancels updated methane standards and climate accounting; and the climate consequences of expanded oil and gas development and the Keystone pipeline fall on everyone. The end date depends on a foreign army's movements, so the freeze could last as long as the war does.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to weaker air and climate rules

drawbacks.text: Suspending the EPA's ozone and particulate-matter standards decisions would leave the public without the air-quality limits on smog and soot that those reviews underpin [S3].

The bill's end date is tied to Russia withdrawing all troops from Ukraine — a decision entirely outside U.S. control — so the regulatory freeze could continue indefinitely for as long as the war lasts [S3].

Reverting all covered actions to their January 19, 2021 status mid-stream would wipe out updated methane standards and the government's social cost of carbon estimates, creating regulatory whiplash for agencies, courts, and businesses alike [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the consumer-price promise is speculative: crude oil is priced on world markets, so additional U.S. leasing and permitting does not reliably or quickly lower what American drivers and homeowners pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — cheaper energy during a wartime price spike — rests on an indirect mechanism, since world oil prices, not U.S. permitting alone, set what consumers pay. Its concrete, immediate effects run the other way: regulatory certainty and cost relief for oil and gas producers, a statutory permit for the Keystone pipeline, and the suspension of smog, soot, methane, and climate rules whose costs fall on the public's health and environment. As drafted, the benefits to ordinary consumers are speculative while the costs to them are specific and open-ended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill on March 10, 2022, about two weeks after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, with Senators Cornyn and Sullivan as cosponsors — 3 of 50 Senate Republicans in total [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which took no further action on it [S5].
No floor vote, committee vote, or hearing appears anywhere in the bill's action history, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the air-quality, methane, and climate rules the bill would have suspended, since none of its deregulation took effect. Oil and gas producers did not get the regulatory freeze, the Keystone permit revival, or the lending protections they sought from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People kept existing air and climate rules

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor was a Republican — Senator Lankford plus 3 of 50 Senate Republicans as cosponsors — and no votes were ever held, so the bill never drew Democratic support or opposition on the record.

industries.note: The bill would suspend the executive orders, EPA methane and air-quality rules, FERC climate reviews, and social cost of carbon estimates that raise the industry's costs, and bar financial regulators from restricting its access to bank capital. Its gain comes at the expense of air-quality and climate protections for the public, though its price-relief argument for consumers was speculative since oil is priced globally.

The bill would statutorily restore the 2019 border-crossing permit that the pipeline needed after its administrative revocation, allowing construction to resume without further approvals. That revives a project whose expanded oil-sands transport carries long-term climate costs for the public.

The bill would prohibit the Federal Reserve and other financial regulators from restricting lending to oil and gas companies, keeping a large lending business open to banks. The public cost is indirect: climate-risk rules for that lending would stay off the table.
